messages.subject: Plots and Command Output?
messages.body_plain:
knitr’s,

I would like to have a chunk that echos all R commands, shows the results that would be printed to the console below the R commands, but “saves” the graphs to be used in an \includegraphics call and does not print the graphs immediately after the R command that constructs the graph.  I can’t seem to find the right combination of include=, results=, echo=, etc. that will result in what I want.  I guess my question is … is it possible to suppress the immediate showing of graphics while still allowing the immediate showing of R console output within the same chunk?

In the attached example, I would like the results from chunk 3 with the exception that the histogram immediately following hist() (the unlabeled histogram) would not appear.

Any thoughts on how to accomplish this task would be greatly appreciated.  Thank you in advance.

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Plots and Command Output?
messages.body_plain:
If you'd like the figures not to appear in the resulting pdf at all, I think you'll want to redefine plot at the beginning of your script:

    knit_hooks$set(plot = function(x, options) "")

e.g. I add this command before calling knit() when I want to compile a pdf where images are not embedded (e.g. for journals that require this).  Could probably be set chunk by chunk if necessary, but I'm guessing you want this to be the global behavior.

hth,

Carl

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] each line on its own page in output
messages.subject_clean: [knitr] each line on its own page in output
messages.body_plain:
It turns out to be a problem of the kframe environment again
(http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/framed/). The framed package does not
work well with the lineno package. If you comment out %\linenumbers,
everything works fine.

The other solution is to use the listings package by putting a chunk
like this in your document:

<<setup, include=FALSE>>=
render_listings()
@

In most cases the listings package is more robust. The framed package
is quite fragile.

Regards,
Yihui
--

messages.subject: encoding handling?
messages.body_plain:
Hi! I had quite the adventure with knitr today, when I found that
things were working differently when I ran them in Rstudio (as normal)
as compared to running them as part of knitting to HTML. After much
futzing around, I found the problem was an en dash in one of my input
files, which read into R just fine with "read.csv('filename.txt')" but
when running that during the knit, the file quit loading precisely at
the en dash (octal \226, emphatically NOT a regular ASCII hyphen). Are
the encoding assumptions inside the knitting environment different
somehow? It seems, from my fairly ignorant position, that it would be
nice to have things work when knitting exactly as they do when
otherwise using R. Is there a reason for this behavior, or some
setting that I ought to be setting anyway, or something like that?
Thanks for all the awesomeness of knitr,

- Aaron

Encoding is always a pain under the OS which does not use UTF8
consistently (aka Windows). Your Rnw or Rmd file has its own encoding,
and the CSV file seems to have another type of encoding. RStudio
respects the encoding of your source file, but the CSV file is really
out of its control (there is no reliable way to detect the encoding of
a file automatically).

A similar issue has been brought forward before:
https://github.com/yihui/knitr/issues/256#issuecomment-5938451

Or see the fileEncoding/encoding arguments in ?read.csv

Regards,
Yihui

>>
>> The input of child files into the main document is great for organization,

>> you're working on a piece and it's isolated from the rest of a big main

>>

>> suggest a simple solution.
>>
>> We could have an option for a parent in the child's \SweaveOpts, or as a

>> -------- child-doc.Rnw --------
>> \SweaveOpts{parent=../main.Rnw}

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] no graph, bibliography error
messages.body_plain:
You are using the PNG device, and latex does not support PNG (there
might be packages which I do not know); pdflatex supports PNG images.

My suggestion to you is to spend _a few years_ learning LaTeX before
using it with knitr, otherwise you can start with R Markdown
(http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/minimal/). Of course it does not take
years to be able to answer your question below, but I'm sure you will
have tons of questions later since you do not seem to know the
difference between latex and pdflatex. I'm still learning LaTeX after
8 years of using it. It is worth the efforts but may sound scary to
some users. I just do not want to answer pure LaTeX questions; it is
too much burden for me.

Back to your question: if you have to use latex at all (it is rare
nowadays), you have to use eps images, which corresponds to
dev='postscript' in knitr. But pdflatex does not support eps...

Regards,
Yihui

messages.subject: knitr -> LaTeX -> HTML
messages.body_plain:
I am getting closer in my quest to convert knitr-style Sweave -> LaTeX
-> HTML in a clean way.  (I know Yihui and a lot of power users here
would prefer to use Markdown as a starting point, and that makes sense a
lot of the time -- but I have some fairly complicated documents that I
really do want to use LaTeX+R chunks (rather than Markdown+R chunks) to
write, and I would still like to produce HTML as an alternative output
format to PDF ...)

  Here's a sample document that shows how far I've gotten:

http://www.math.mcmaster.ca/bolker/misc/knitr_listings_test.Rnw
http://www.math.mcmaster.ca/bolker/misc/knitr_listings_test.html
http://www.math.mcmaster.ca/bolker/misc/knitr_listings_test.pdf

 This is using render_listings() as advised by Yihui, and using htlatex
to convert from LaTeX to HTML.

 My only problems at the moment (with this very simple document --
perhaps I will have more trouble with something more complex ...) are

(1) htlatex chokes slightly on the '<-' expression inside S input chunks
-- it does give the right output in the end, and I can hit 's' to skip
over errors, but if possible it would be nice to figure out how to make
the errors go away.

(2) the HTML output isn't very beautiful -- tried to fix this with some
CSS magic found in one of the links referred to in my document, but no
luck yet.

(3) I prefer the native syntax highlighting generated in 'standard'
knitr to the render_listings()-style output (but this is looking a gift
horse in the mouth, and I can certainly live with it.

  I realize this is pretty obscure, but maybe someone has an idea (and
maybe this will be useful to someone else).  I'm a little out of my
depth in dealing with the multiple layers here [knitr/listings
package/htlatex] (I haven't cc'd Frank Harrell on this because I don't
want to bug him, but Frank, if you're reading this, I can imagine that
you would have some ideas ...)

  thanks
    Ben Bolker

[ snip ]

I have a similar quest:

1. Write once!. I don't care what the initial authoring format is (LyX
or Markdown, for example) as long as I have a reasonable continuous
integration workflow. I write and my "reproducible research"
compendium of code, text and data is continuously built and tested and
the output documents continuously updated and viewable.

2. Four outputs that pass validation suites and that look good: PDF,
EPUB, MOBI and HTML5 with all the bells and whistles, interactivity,
etc.. Again, this must all be automated in the tradition of
reproducible research. The ideal case would be an HTML5 full-featured
output as the "prime" document with the others derived from it by a
mechanical reduction process.

3. Ability to mix R with Perl and bash scripts in the compendium. Most
everything is in R, but I have quite a bit of Twitter interface code
that uses Perl and quite a few bash scripts that install OS-level
dependencies.

I'm almost there (on Fedora Linux; Windows is hopeless, I can't afford
a Mac and no matter which Linux I pick, some components need to be
built from source rather than from the distro's repositories). I write
now in LyX and run a bash script using ImageMagick, Sigil, epubcheck
and Calibre "every so often" to export LyX to PDF and HTML and then do
the EPUB / MOBI reformatting. The document is currently using "knitr",
not "Sweave". There are a few manual steps in this but I'm pretty sure
they can be automated, or at least won't be so annoying when I have a
continuous integration toolchain.

I'm hoping to migrate this to RStudio / Markdown this week and
complete the continuous integration coding. There's little reason not
to do the continuous integration and test code in R. It's not as
"pretty" as Ruby, Python, Perl or bash but it will do the job.

The two stumbling blocks are

1. RStudio "knit to HTML" embeds the image as a Base64 object directly
in the HTML. I'm sure there's a "hook" to get it into its own file,
but I haven't found it yet. I need the image separate because it needs
to be full-size in the PDF and HTML5 output but scaled down via
ImageMagick for the EPUB and MOBI.

2. There doesn't seem to be a "knit to HTML *and* PDF". The best I've
found so far is to generate an Rnw as an intermediate.

I think I can do most of this with hooks, but I'm looking at some
other tools that seem to have more built-in infrastructure. My
preference is to acquire code rather than write it. ;-)

--

http://j.mp/CompJournStudio

messages.subject: late appearance of ggplots from for loop
messages.subject_clean: late appearance of ggplots from for loop
messages.body_plain:
Hi! I'm trying to generate a bunch of plots with some supporting text for each. I'm doing it in a for loop. Because I need to have other text, which could be arbitrarily long, pulled in before and after each plot, I can't really use plot text or faceting for this. The problem I'm having is that the first plot comes out where the second plot should be, and so on. Here's a very simple illustration:

```{r demo, results='asis', echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
data <- data.frame(rnorm(1000),rep(letters, len=1000))
names(data) <- c("value","category")
for (i in 1:6) {
  cat(paste("#",LETTERS[i],"\n"))
  print(ggplot(subset(data,category==letters[i]), aes(x=value)) + geom_histogram())
  cat("\n")
}
```

This yields results that look like this when rendered in the browser:

A
B
[plot a]
C
[plot b]
D
[plot c]
E
[plot d]
F
[plot e]
[plot f]

I really want [plot a] to appear right after A. I've tried things like Sys.sleep(0) or dev.flush() after the print(), just because I was trying anything I could find. Am I missing a chunk option I ought to have in there or something? How can this be fixed?

Thanks,

- Aaron
